entries.modern_form: NP bāzār < MP wāzār (Book Pahlavi wʾCʾl) < Old Iranian *wahā-čaraņa- 'place of sale, trade-traffic' (PIE *wes- 'buy, sell' + *kʷel- 'turn, move about'); NOT Skt sabhā 'assembly' / OP *abā-čari-
entries.note: Nourai here reproduces verbatim Darmesteter's 1883 etymology (Études iraniennes II, article 'ABÂCARI', pp.129-131): OP abācari- = abā (= Skt sabhā 'lieu de réunion') + cari (abstract of car- 'to go'), hence 'comitii locus', giving NP bāzār. That analysis was rejected within a decade and has not been revived. (a) Horn, Grundriss no.166 (p.38) — the very page Nourai cites at node #4 — says flatly 'Wegen phlv. č ist die Zusammenstellung mit ap. abācaris unmöglich' ('because of the Pahlavi č the connection with OP abācaris is impossible'), and reports in the same footnote that Bartholomae (Litbl. f. or. Phil. I,19) had already argued against Darmesteter's abā = sabhā and proposed instead a(m)bācaris 'Wasserwerk, Brunnen'. (b) The Old Persian hapax of DB I.64 is read abicariš (abi- not abā-) by Kent, Old Persian, Lex. s.v., who glosses it 'pasture lands' (abi- + čar- 'to graze', cf. NP čarīdan); Bartholomae, AiW s.v. māniya-, cites it and says 'Et. und eig. Bed. unsicher'. (c) Phonologically the Iranian reflex of PIIr *sabhā keeps h-: Mann, IEC s.v. sebh- gives 'Av. haba, f.' beside 'Skt. sabha, f. company, meeting-place'; and Walde-Pokorny (Bd. II, root 2. bhā- 'sprechen') derive sabhā itself from *bhā- 'speak' (*'Zusammensprechen'), not from a root 'assemble'. (d) The consensus etymology since Watkins/AHD is *wahā-čaraņa-, i.e. Av. vahā- / NP bahā 'price, sale' (PIE *wes-no-, Pokorny 1173) + *čaraņa- (PIE *kʷel-, which is exactly the 'Kwel' cross-reference Nourai himself puts on node #1). Buck (SYN 11.85) already flagged the older etymology as unsettled ('etym.? Horn 166'). The language label is also odd: 'Sanskrit / Old Persian' pairs a real Sanskrit word (sabhā 'assembly hall') with a disputed reading of an Old Persian hapax.

ref_check.note: BQT_v1_pages.txt ↵-leaf 438 (the leaf carries 'شه از صفحهٔ ۲۱۷' = 'continued from p.217', so this is printed p.218). Mo'in's footnote s.v. بازار: 'بازار - در پهلوی [و در: هوجستان واچار = سوق‌الاحواز، رک: خوزستان] … محل خرید و فروش کالا و خوراک و پوشاک. لغت فرانسه bazar از پرتقالی گرفته شده و پرتغالیان نیز از ایرانیان گرفته‌اند'. So BQT:218 supports Pahlavi wāčār > NP bāzār (and the Hozēstān wāčār = Sūq al-Ahwāz attestation), but says nothing about Sanskrit sabhā or an Old Persian abācari-, and routes the European word through Portuguese, not Turkish/Italian.

DRM.txt leaves 516-517 = Études iraniennes t. II pp.131-132 (printed page numbers '131' and '132' visible in the OCR; the article 'ABÂCARI' begins on p.129, which is why Nourai cites 129). Darmesteter: 'abâcari- … devait donner: bazar ou bâzâr: on reconnaît le persan بازار … Il se décompose naturellement en abâ et cari; dans cari on reconnaît le substantif qui a donné au persan le suffixe de lieu … c'est sans doute un abstrait de car, aller … abâ semble être un exemple analogue; ce serait le sanscrit sabhâ, lieu de réunion, réunion. L'abâcari, le bâzâr, est donc littéralement comitii locus.' Footnote: 'Cf. le sanscrit sabhâ-cara, qui se rend à la réunion, au conseil.' This is exactly Nourai's root box and node #1 — but it is an 1883 proposal that Horn and Bartholomae rejected.

LKT.txt leaf ~50, entry no. 278 (printed p.24): '[Pers. bāzār] ‘Markt’ [Horn NpEt S.38, Nr.166]. Das Wort wurde im 17. Jahrhundert durch Reisende zunächst mit Bezug auf orientalische Verhältnisse eingeführt und drang dann … in alle europäischen Sprachen ein: frz. pg. sp. bazar, it. bazar, bazzar … engl. bazar, bazaar …'. Lokotsch documents the European spread from Persian, but gives no Sanskrit/Old Persian root at all — he simply refers the etymology to Horn no.166, which denies the abācari- connection.

nodes.derivation: The form exists only as one hapax in Darius' Bisotun inscription, DB I.64: 'adām niyāčam kārahyā abičariš gaiθāmčā māniyamčā viθbiščā …'. Darmesteter (Ét. ir. II 129-131) read it abācari-, split it abā + cari-, equated abā with Skt sabhā 'assembly' (assuming exceptional loss of Iranian h- < s-, on the analogy of OP θā-ati for θāhati) and cari- with an abstract of car- 'to go', giving 'place where one goes to assemble' = comitii locus, whence NP bāzār. Kent (Old Persian, Lex.) instead reads abičariš (abi- + čar- 'to move, graze'), acc. of an s-stem, and translates DB I.64 'I restored to the people the pastures and the herds, the household property and the houses', i.e. 'pasture lands' — a reading now standard. Bartholomae (AiW s.v. māniya-) quotes the word and says 'Et. und eig. Bed. unsicher'. Phonetically the Iranian outcome of *sabhā would be *habā- (Av. haba-, Mann IEC s.v. sebh-), so the loss of h- is ad hoc; and Horn adds the decisive objection that Pahlavi wāčār has č, which cannot continue an OP -c- ([ts]/[s]) of abācari-. So the node's gloss ('place of assembly') and its role as the ancestor of bāzār are both rejected by modern Iranian scholarship.

consulted.note: 'abicariš DB 1.64f, word of uncertain form and meaning, probably asn. of s-stem, to abi- + root car- ‘move, go’ … giving, in association [with gaiθā and māniya], a meaning ‘pasture lands’, cf. Bartholomae quotes 'kārahya abicaris gaiθamca … Bh. I.14' and comments 'Et. und eig. Bed. unsicher' — he registers the word but refuses both the reading abā- and the meaning 'assembly'.

Mann: 'sebh-, sebhi (sobh-) ‘self; like; kin…’ … Skt. cf. sabha, f. ‘company, meeting-place’; Av. haba, f. id.; … Go. sibja, f. ‘kinship’'. The Iranian cognate of sabhā is haba- WITH h-, so an Old Persian abā- from this root is not expected.
'Ai. wahrscheinlich in sabha „Versammlung“ (*„Zusammensprechen“…)' — Walde-Pokorny put Skt sabhā under *bhā- 'to speak' with sa-, not under any root 'assemble'.
Pokorny's IEW has no lemma for Skt sabhā and no Iranian abā- 'assembly'; the only 'sabha' hits are the unrelated -ṣabha of ṛṣabhá- 'bull'.

'Wegen phlv. č ist die Zusammenstellung mit ap. abācaris unmöglich.' Footnote: '… zu ai. sabhā- ‘Sippe’, das auch schon Darmesteter Ét. ir. II,131 in abā gesucht und wogegen Bartholomae, Litbl. f. or. Phil. I,19 sich ausgesprochen hatte.'

nodes.derivation: The Middle Persian word itself is well attested and correctly given: Book Pahlavi wʾCʾl = wāzār 'market' (Manichaean MP wʾCʾr-), best known from the place-name Hūzēstān wāzār 'the market of Khuzistan', the old name of Ahvāz, rendered in Arabic Sūq al-Ahwāz (Mujmal al-tawārīkh; Tabari, tr. Nöldeke p.13 n.3), and borrowed early into Armenian as vačaṛ, vačaṛakan, vačaṛik. What is disputed is the ARROW: wāzār cannot come from OP abācari-, because Pahlavi č cannot continue OP c, and because the word's real ancestor is Old Iranian *wahā-čaraņa- 'trade-circulation, place of sale' — *wahā- 'sale, price' (Av. vahā-, NP bahā; PIE *wes-no-, Pokorny 1173) + *čaraņa- 'going about' (PIE *kʷel-). Loss of the intervocalic -ņ- and contraction give MP wāzār; Iranian *č > z before the following vowel is regular in this compound (cf. NP bahā). Nourai's 'trade center' gloss is right; his parentage is not.

nodes.derivation: NP bāzār 'market' is the regular inherited continuation of MP wāzār: initial Middle Persian w- > NP b- (the standard change, cf. MP wād > NP bād 'wind', MP wed > NP bed 'willow'), the rest unchanged. It is attested from the earliest New Persian poetry onward (the verse Nourai quotes is Vaḥši Bāfqi, 16th c.). From Persian the word was lent out in every direction: Armenian vačaṛ, Aramaic/Talmudic, Arabic bāzār, Ottoman Turkish bāzār/pazar, Hindi-Urdu bāzār, Malay pasar, and thence the European family. Only the pre-Middle-Persian step (node #1) is in doubt; this node is not.

nodes.derivation: 'Merchant' is right and the connection with bāzār is right, but the word was not coined in New Persian: MacKenzie records MP wāzāraġān [wʾCʾlkʾn], Manichaean MP wʾCʾrgʾn 'merchant', so NP bāzargān/bāzergān is inherited alongside bāzār rather than derived from it in Persian. Darmesteter (Ét. ir. I §217) explains the morphology: an adjective in -ān was added to a stem *bāzārak 'merchant', giving bāzāragān; once *bāzārak dropped out of use the word 'semble formé de bazar, par suffixe gān', which is how the productive Persian suffix -gān arose. The vowel of the second syllable is shortened in bāzargān < bāzāragān by regular medial reduction. The abstract bāzargānī 'trade' continues MP wāzāraġānīh.

nodes.derivation: Empty pass-through node: Ottoman Turkish بازار bāzār, with the regular Turkish devoicing of the initial in the popular form pazar 'market; Sunday (market-day)', borrowed from Persian bāzār during the long Persianate phase of Ottoman/Seljuq lexis. Turkish is the vehicle by which the word reached the Balkans and the Mediterranean (Bulgarian/Serbian pazar, Modern Greek παζάρι), and the 1976 AHD, Etymonline and Nourai all make it the link between Persian and Italian. Hobson-Jobson's early Genoese attestation (c.1340) suggests direct Levantine trade contact could also have carried it, so Turkish is the likely but not the only possible conduit.

nodes.derivation: Empty pass-through node: Italian bazarra / bazzarro / bazarro 'market', with the doubling and the -a/-o ending typical of Italian adaptations of Levantine words. It is attested strikingly early: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti's merchant handbook (c.1340) already lists Bazarra as the Genoese word for 'market-place', and the Venetian envoys to Persia use it — Ambrogio Contarini 1474 'con bazzari come quello', Giosafat Barbaro 1478 'un ricco mercante in bazarro'. Italian bazzarare 'to cheat' is a derivative. From Italian the word passed to English (1580s) and, in parallel, French bazar.

nodes.derivation: English bazaar is first recorded in the 1580s in accounts of the East, taken from Italian bazarra (so Etymonline and the 1976 AHD, which spell the chain out as Italian bazarra < Turkish pazar < Persian bāzār < Pahlavi vacar < Old Iranian *vahā-čarana 'sale, traffic'). The spelling with -aar and the stress bə-ZÄR follow the Persian; the senses 'fancy fair for charity' (19th c.) and 'large fancy store' are English developments. Anglo-Indian usage reinforced the word in the 18th-19th c. through Hindi-Urdu bāzār.

(The local AHD_watkins1985.txt has 'wes-1. To buy. … [Pok. 8. wes- 1173]' but, being only the root appendix, lists no bazaar; Nourai's AHD page numbers are the 1976 appendix, whose bazaar entry also read 'Italian bazarra, from Turkish pazar, from Persian bāzār'.)

entries.note: The root box is right: ʕ-b-r 'to cross over' is a genuine common-Semitic root (Arabic ʕabara, Hebrew ʕāḇar, Aramaic/Syriac ʕăḇar, Akkadian ebēru, Old South Arabian ʕbr 'to transgress', Geʿez), and the Hebrew branch (ʕibrī 'Hebrew' = 'he from across the river' > Aram. ʕibray > Gk Ἑβραῖος > Lat. Hebraeus > English Hebrew) is Klein's entry almost word for word. The one contested limb is the middle one: the claim that Arabic ʕ-r-b (ʕarab 'Arab') is a metathesised ('distorted') form of ʕ-b-r, making 'Arab' and 'Hebrew' the same word. Nourai's own source Bahar (SBK) reports that as the view of 'modern scholars', but Nourai's other own source Klein (KLN:98) does NOT: Klein derives ʕarab from the sense 'desert' (Heb. ʕărāḇāh), and current handbooks list the ʕ-b-r metathesis as only one of several competing hypotheses ('west, sunset', 'desert', 'mingle', 'merchant', 'raven'). Two smaller drawing faults: the Latin stage (L. Arabs, acc. Arabem) is missing between Greek and French for 'Arab', and the Old French/Middle English stage (OF Ebreu > ME Ebreu, H- restored in the 16th c.) is missing between Latin and English for 'Hebrew'.

nodes.derivation: Arabic عبر ʕ-b-r is the direct Arabic continuation of Proto-Semitic *ʕabar- 'to cross'; the form Nourai transliterates 'abara' is the 3 m.sg. perfect عَبَرَ ʕabara 'he crossed, traversed, forded' (his gloss 'he passes across' should be a past, as in Klein's 'he passed across'). Same root: عَبْر ʕabr 'crossing', عِبْرَة ʕibra 'lesson' (< 'what one crosses over to'), عَبَّرَ ʕabbara 'to express, interpret'. Cognates: Hebrew עָבַר ʕāḇar, Akkadian ebēru, OSA ʕbr.

consulted.note: See above; Klein makes Arabic ʕabara a cognate (not a source) of Hebrew ʕāḇar, which is what a common Semitic root box means.

nodes.derivation: Persian عبور obūr is the Arabic verbal noun (maṣdar) عُبُور ʕubūr, pattern fuʕūl, of ʕabara 'to cross', taken into Persian with the usual Persian pronunciation of the Arabic ʕu- as o- and no change of consonants. The extras Nourai prints are all further ʕ-b-r derivatives borrowed alongside it: عابر ʕābir 'one who crosses, passer-by' (active participle fāʕil), معبر maʕbar 'crossing-place, ford' (noun of place mafʕal), pl. معابر maʕābir. Direction of borrowing is Arabic > Persian (post-conquest lexical Arabising), not a round trip.

nodes.derivation: Nourai (following Bahar) treats عرب ʕ-r-b as a metathesised 'distortion' of عبر ʕ-b-r, so that 'to cross the desert' > 'to dwell in the desert'. Metathesis of the 2nd and 3rd radicals is a real Semitic phenomenon and the equation ʕ-b-r ~ ʕ-r-b was current in 19th-/early-20th-c. Semitic philology (Bahar cites Tārīḫ al-luġāt al-sāmiyya pp.79-81 for it). Modern reference works do not accept it as established: they treat ʕ-r-b as an independent root whose recorded senses are 'west, sunset' (cf. Akk. erēbu 'to enter, to set'), 'desert, steppe' (Heb. עֲרָבָה ʕărāḇāh), 'to mix, mingle', 'merchant' and 'raven', and list the ʕ-b-r derivation only as one alleged hypothesis among these. Decisively for this chart, the very reference Nourai cites for the next node — Klein p.98 — chooses a different origin. So the arrow ʕ-b-r > ʕ-r-b is a minority view presented here as fact.

ref_check.note: SBK.txt ll.4035-4046 (Bahar's chapter on the Semitic peoples and the Phoenician script, printed p. ~69): 'نام «عبری» از مادهٔ «عبر» و بمعنی عبور و حرکت و اشاره بصحرانوردی آن طایفه است' and, decisively, 'وعلمای معاصر ترجیح میدهند که عبری را از مادهٔ عبور گرفته … چنانکه «عرب» را هم از همین [ماده] و بهمان معنی میدانند و ثلاثی مجرد … «عبر» و «عرب» را یکی دانند که بقاعدهٔ قلب لغات اختلاف یافته است' ('… they hold the triliteral roots ʕ-b-r and ʕ-r-b to be one and the same, differentiated by the rule of metathesis'), with the footnote 'رک: تاریخ اللغات السامیه ص ۷۹-۸۰-۸۱ وبعدها'. This is Nourai's claim verbatim. (SBK.txt carries no page breaks; the passage sits in the section that in the 1st ed. runs pp. ~66-72, so p.69 is consistent but could not be confirmed to the page.)

nodes.derivation: The word and the gloss are correct: عَرَب ʕarab is the collective 'the Arabs', and أَعْرَاب aʕrāb (the form Nourai transliterates 'a`rab') is its plural used specifically of the desert-dwelling Bedouin, as opposed to settled ʕarab — the distinction the Qurʼān itself draws (S. 9:97 al-aʕrāb). Both are formations on the root ʕ-r-b, so the arrow from node #3 is right as a root-to-derivative step; what is disputed is only where that root itself comes from (see node #3). Klein glosses ʕarab 'inhabitant of the desert', matching Nourai's 'desert dweller, Arab'.

nodes.derivation: Persian عرب ʕarab is a straight lexical borrowing of the Arabic collective عَرَب, unchanged in consonants and written with ع in the Arabic manner (pronounced arab in Persian, the ʕayn being lost). The three extras are likewise Arabic derivatives of ʕ-r-b borrowed wholesale: إعراب eʕrāb, form-IV verbal noun, 'making (speech) Arabic clear' → the technical term for the inflectional vowels/case-endings of Arabic grammar; أعرابی aʕrābī, nisba to aʕrāb, 'a Bedouin'; معرّب muʕarrab, passive participle of form II ʕarraba, 'Arabicised (word)' — the standard term in Persian and Arabic philology for a loanword adapted into Arabic.

Ἄραβος Árabos, with the country-name Ἀραβία Arabía, taken from the Semitic ethnonym ʕarab (already Assyrian Ḵur-ba-a-a / Aribi in the 9th-8th c. The chart is right that French mediates, but it omits the Latin stage that both Klein and Etymonline insert: Greek Ἄραψ/Ἄραβος was borrowed into Latin as Arabs, acc. Arabem, and it is the Latin accusative (the regular input to Old French nouns) that yields OF Arabe/Arabi — Greek could not have given French directly. Hence 'plausible' rather than 'confirmed': the route is compatible with the sources but a link is missing.

nodes.derivation: English Arab is attested from the late 14th century, borrowed from Old French Arabe/Arabi (Latin Arabem, Greek Ἄραψ, Arabic ʕarab). Derivatives followed the same route: Arabic (adj.) from OF, from L. Arabicus; arabesque from French/Italian arabesco. The 19th-c. sense 'street Arab, homeless little wanderer' (1848) is a metaphor on Bedouin nomadism, not a separate word.

nodes.derivation: Hebrew עָבַר ʕāḇar 'he passed over, crossed' is the direct Hebrew reflex of Proto-Semitic *ʕabar-; from its noun עֵבֶר ʕēḇer 'region across, the other side' is formed the gentilic עִבְרִי ʕiḇrī 'Hebrew', literally 'he (who came) from across (the River)' — the epithet used of Abram in Gen. 14:13 and of the Israelites in the Joseph and Exodus narratives, characteristically in the mouths of foreigners. Whether 'the River' is the Euphrates or the Jordan is undecided; Klein and Etymonline both note the possibility that it simply meant 'immigrant, one from the other side', and Klein cross-refers to the Amarna-age Ḫabiru. Nourai's gloss for ʕiḇrī reproduces this explanation.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966 p.712 s.v. Hebrew: 'fr. Heb. ‘ibhrī, ‘Hebrew’, lit. ‘he who came from across (the River)’, fr. ‘ibher, ‘region across, side’, from the stem of ‘abhar, ‘he passed across or over’ … Cp. Habiru.' Nourai's two words and both glosses come straight from here.

consulted.note: As quoted; Klein also lists the cognate nouns Heb. ‘ebhrāh 'fury' (lit. 'overflow') and ma‘ăbhār 'ford, pass' from the same stem.

nodes.derivation: Aramaic עִבְרַי ʕiḇray / ʕeḇray (Syriac ʕeḇrāyā) is the Aramaic gentilic corresponding to Hebrew ʕiḇrī, with the Aramaic nisba ending -ay for Hebrew -ī. It is the form that stood behind the Greek transcription, since Greek Ἑβραῖος has -ai- reflecting Aramaic -ay, not Hebrew -ī — which is Klein's and Wiktionary's reason for inserting an Aramaic stage at all. Aramaic was the everyday language of Palestinian Jewry in the Hellenistic period, so the mediation is historically as well as phonetically expected.

nodes.derivation: Empty pass-through node: Arabic عِبْرِيّ ʕibrī and عِبْرَانِيّ ʕibrānī 'Hebrew (language, person)'. Because the root ʕ-b-r exists in Arabic in its own right, the Arabic word could in principle be a native formation; but the reference of the nisba to the people, and above all the -ān- of ʕibrānī, point to a calque or borrowing on the Aramaic/Syriac ʕeḇrāyā (with Aramaic -āyā reanalysed and re-suffixed with Arabic -ī), which is how the biblical vocabulary generally entered Arabic — through Syriac-speaking Christians and Jews. The route drawn (Hebrew > Aramaic > Arabic) is therefore likely, but none of the works checked (Fraenkel's Aramaic loanwords in Arabic, Jeffery's Foreign Vocabulary of the Qurʼān, Klein) states it, so it stands as plausible rather than documented.

nodes.derivation: Both Persian words are Arabic nisbas borrowed unchanged: عبری ebrī and its extended doublet عبرانی ebrānī, both 'Hebrew (person, language)'. Persian keeps the Arabic spelling with ع and simply drops the ʕayn in pronunciation; the choice between the two is stylistic, ebrānī being the commoner in Persian for the language. Note that these do NOT continue any Persian root — they are part of the general post-conquest importation of Arabic religious/ethnographic vocabulary.

nodes.derivation: Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος Hebraîos, borrowed from Aramaic ʕiḇray (the -ai- of the Greek renders Aramaic -ay), with the Greek adjectival/ethnic ending -ος. It is the word of the Septuagint and of Hellenistic Jewish writers (Philo, Josephus) and of the New Testament (e.g. 2 Cor. 11:22, Phil. 3:5, and the title προς Ἑβραίους), which is how it reached Latin Christendom. The rough breathing gives the initial H- that Latin and, eventually, English restore.

nodes.derivation: Latin Hebraeus (also Hebraicus 'Hebrew, in Hebrew'), a Christian-Latin transcription of Greek Ἑβραῖος with -αι- rendered by -ae- and the rough breathing by H-. It is the form of the Vetus Latina and of Jerome's Vulgate (Epistula ad Hebraeos; hebraice 'in Hebrew'), and it is from the Latin of the Church that the word entered all the Western vernaculars.

nodes.derivation: English Hebrew is right as the end of the chain, but not straight from Latin: the actual route is Latin Hebraeus > Old French Ebreu / Ebrieu > Middle English Ebreu (adj. in late Old English; the noun for the language c.1200; of the people by the late 14th c.), and the H- was restored in English spelling only in the 16th century under the influence of the Latin form. The chart's Latin > English arrow therefore compresses two attested stages; the etymology is otherwise exactly Klein's. Hence 'plausible' rather than 'confirmed'.
